newsitem.title: UK: Regulator to probe BT's UK obligations post-merger.
newsitem.headline: Regulator to probe BT's UK obligations post-merger.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc's obligations to its domestic market will come under the spotlight should its proposed merger with U.S. giant MCI go ahead, a telecommunications regulator warned on Wednesday.

Oftel director general Donald Cruickshank told a Trade and Industry Select committee in parliament that some action may be needed to ensure BT, with a new global outlook, did not neglect the small British consumer.
"My present judgement is that some amendments to BT's licenCe may be necessary to safeguard UK consumers," he said.

But subject to those changes, he said the merger would be highly desirable for the telecommunications market and for the British economy as a whole. Cruickshank said the merger process was essentially the concern of European Union and United States regulatory authorities.
But with the merger set to produce a global telecommunications giant, those officials are unlikely to consider the needs of the British consumer in isolation.
"We have yet to think through the details of our review," Cruickshank said.

The planned $20 billion merger between the two telecommunications giants was submitted to the European Commission for clearance in December under the EU's merger rules which ban the creation or strengthening of dominant positions.
Cruickshank said of most concern to Oftel were some 16 million domestic consumers who do not use telecommunications to any great extent.

It is that sort of consumer, who perhaps makes few international calls and therefore does not benefit from the competitions offered by foreign telecommunications operators, whose interests needed most defending, he said.
Although the British telecoms market has been opened up to competition, allowing in various cable operators, BT still runs about 90 percent of all exchange lines.
"BT has over the years continued with a financial capacity inappropriate to its capital needs," Cruickshank said. "Now it is being used, my concern is to see it is done with no harm to UK consumers."
